Habibie, South Tangerang 15314, Indonesia We examine electron and muon anomalous magnetic dipole moments within a radiative neutrino mass model featuring TeVscale scalar leptoquarks S(3, 1, −1/3) and R(3, 2, 1/6). We utilize textures with decoupling electron and muon sectors, so that both electron and muon anomalous magnetic dipole moments could receive internal chiral enhancements from different heavy uptype quarks while in the same time evading the stringent µ →eγ constraint. A successful fit to neutrino oscillation data requires the simultaneous presence of oneand twoloop neutrino mass contributions. This severely constrains the parameter space of the model, which results in a negligible new physics correction to the muon g −2. The electron g −2 discrepancy implied by the rubidium experiment, on the other hand, can be resolved within 2σ uncertainty provided that neutrino mass ordering is inverted. Leptonflavorviolating tau decay rates, such as τ →eγ and τ →3e, are predicted to be within the sensitivities of nextgeneration experiments. I. INTRODUCTION The massive nature of neutrinos remains the only direct experimental evidence for physics beyond the Standard Model (SM). However, the dynamical origin of neutrino masses is still unknown and has been extensively studied even before the discovery of neutrino oscillations. While the canonical seesaw mechanism [1] provides a compelling explanation, it postulates new physics at a very high energy scale (i.e., of the order 1014 GeV), far beyond any foreseeable experimental reach. An alternative and more testable approach is found in radiative neutrino mass models, in which neutrino masses are induced by higherorder quantum loop corrections at a lower energy scale [2–4]. These models often predict observable rates for leptonflavorviolating decays that can be probed by nextgeneration experiments, providing an independent cross check. See Refs. [5, 6] for reviews on this subject. Beside neutrino masses, other observational data can be employed to test the SM. These include precision measurements of leptonic anomalous magnetic dipole moments (from now on called lepton g −2), denoted as aℓ≡1 2(g −2)ℓ. For muon g −2, FNAL E989 has reported an unprecedented accuracy at the level of 127 ppb [7, 8], confirming the earlier BNL E821 result [9]. Interpretation of this result requires a firm SM prediction. The determination of the SM value, however, is now ambiguous due to the tension between datadriven and lattice QCD determinations of the hadronic vacuum polarization contribution. While the latter has been solidified by various groups over the last few years [10], the former faces challenges because of the disagreement between recent e+e−→π+π−data from the CMD3 Collaboration [11] and the earlier data. In the 2025 update, the Theory Initiative Group adopts the lattice result to determine the SM prediction. This results in δaµ ≡aexp µ −aSM µ = 38(63) × 10−11 [12], which

In the 2025 update, the Theory Initiative Group adopts the lattice result to determine the SM prediction. This results in δaµ ≡aexp µ −aSM µ = 38(63) × 10−11 [12], which indicates no statistically significant evidence for new physics. Similar situation is found in the electron g −2. While the experimental value of this quantity has been significantly improved [13] from the previous data [14], this has been overshadowed by the determination of the SM value, hindering a clear interpretation. This is due to the 5σ difference in the measurements of the QED finestructure constant αem, carried out in cesium (Cs) and rubidium (Rb) atoms [15, 16]. These measurements lead to conflicting deviations: δae = (−10±2.6)×10−13 in Cs and δae = (3.5±1.6)×10−13 in Rb, corresponding to −3.8σ and +2.2σ discrepancies, respectively. Although there may be still a room for a new physics, the inconsistency requires further investigation, and at present, we can only treat them as two independent results. In this context, it would be interesting to find models that provide a unified explanation for neutrino masses and the observed values of lepton g −2, particularly those that can have preference over any discrepancy in the electron g −2. Motivated by that, we select a model featuring two scalar leptoquarks S(3, 1, −1/3) and R(3, 2, 1/6). The leptoquark S is known to induce large corrections to lepton g −2 via internal chiral enhancement, as it can couple to both lefthanded and righthanded of the uptype quarks and charged leptons. Moreover, the leading contributions to neutrino ∗bayudirgantara@unhas.ac.id † julio@brin.go.id arXiv:2510.08504v1 [hepph] 9 Oct 2025 masses arise at both oneand twoloop levels. Previous studies on this model, however, focused mostly only on oneloop contributions [17–22]. The twoloop analysis was given in Ref. [23], but it did not include oneloop contributions. To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has simultaneously incorporated both oneand twoloop contributions to neutrino mass within this specific model while also addressing the current lepton g −2 situation. The objective of this paper is twofold. First, we demonstrate how oneand twoloop terms of neutrino masses are equally important to fit neutrino oscillation data. Second, based on the fit, we determine the corrections to lepton g −2. To achieve this goal, we employ particular textures where electron and muon sectors are decoupled, so that the respective anomalous magnetic moments are induced by chiral enhancement from different uptype quarks. This will also avoid the potentially dangerous chirallyenhanced µ →eγ decay.1 We then apply these textures to the neutrino mass formula given in this model. We find that the lightest neutrino is massless although both normal and inverted neutrino mass orderings can be admitted. Neutrino data strongly constrain the parameter space of the model, leading to a small new physics correction to the muon g −2. CONCLUSIONS In this paper, we have presented an analysis on radiative neutrino mass model with two scalar leptoquarks S(3, 1, −1/3) and R(3, 2, 1/6) in the close connection with current lepton g −2 observations. We employed textures with decoupling electron and muon sectors, allowing each anomalous magnetic dipole moment to be induced by different uptype quarks, ensuring no dangerous µ →eγ decay. In minimal scenario that we discussed, a consistency with neutrino oscillation data requires a simultaneous appearance of both oneand twoloop neutrino mass contributions. The model predicts the lightest neutrino to be massless and admits both normal and inverted orderings. The model also establishes a direct connection between neutrino oscillation data and the lepton g −2 values. Consequently, stringent constraints from neutrino data prevent the muon g −2 from getting a large new correction, while allowing a resolution to the discrepancy implied by the Rb experiment within 2σ as long as the neutrino mass ordering is inverted. Furthermore, the model also predicts rates for LFV tau decay processes, such as τ →eγ and τ →3e, that are near to the current limits. Future experimental results, from neutrino oscillations, highluminosity colliders, or LFV searches will be able to confirm or falsify this scenario.
